title: KRDO13 Investigates: Ex Palmer Ridge Wrestling Coach Arrested on Child Sex Crime Charges
body:
A former high‑school wrestling coach in El Pasco County, Colorado, was taken into custody this week on a charge of sexual assault involving a minor, sparking renewed scrutiny of how school districts handle allegations of abuse and prompting calls for tighter oversight of youth sports programs.

Michael Shane Vassar, 38, who led the Palmer Ridge High School wrestling team from 2020 until his resignation in early 2023, was booked into the El Paso County jail on a single count of sexual assault on a child. According to the county’s public records, the alleged offense occurred while Vassar was still employed at the school, and investigators say the victim was a student who participated in the wrestling program. The case is being processed under Colorado’s “one‑in‑a‑position” statute, which classifies sexual contact between an adult and a minor as a felony when the adult holds a position of authority over the child.

The arrest follows a months‑long internal investigation by the El Pasco County School District that began after a parent reported suspicious behavior to school officials in late 2022. District administrators initially placed Vassar on administrative leave while the district’s legal counsel reviewed the allegations. In a statement released by the district’s superintendent, officials said they “cooperated fully with law‑enforcement authorities” and that “the safety of our students remains our highest priority.” The district has since suspended all wrestling activities pending a comprehensive review of its safeguarding policies.

Child‑protection advocates argue that the Vassar case underscores systemic gaps in how schools monitor coaches and other staff who have direct, unsupervised access to minors. “We see a pattern where allegations surface only after a trusted adult has already built a rapport with students,” said Maria Alvarez, director of the Colorado Coalition for Child Safety. “Without clear, enforceable protocols for reporting and independent oversight, schools can inadvertently become safe havens for predatory behavior.” Alvarez cited recent legislation in neighboring states that mandates third‑party auditors for youth sports programs, urging Colorado lawmakers to adopt similar measures.

Legal experts note that the “one‑in‑a‑position” charge carries a potential sentence of up to 12 years in prison, depending on the specifics of the case and any prior criminal history. “Colorado law is clear that an adult who leverages a position of authority to exploit a child faces severe penalties,” explained criminal defense attorney James Whitaker, who has handled several high‑profile child‑abuse cases. Whitaker cautioned that the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Vassar used his coaching role to facilitate the assault, a burden that will hinge on forensic evidence, witness testimony, and the credibility of the victim’s account.

The fallout from the arrest has already impacted the broader athletic community at Palmer Ridge. Parents and athletes voiced frustration on social media, demanding transparency about how the school will protect students moving forward. In response, the school’s athletic director announced the formation of a task force comprising administrators, mental‑health professionals, and external child‑welfare consultants. The task force is slated to deliver a set of recommendations within 60 days, focusing on mandatory background checks for all staff, enhanced training on recognizing grooming behaviors, and stricter supervision ratios during practices and competitions.

As the legal process unfolds, the case serves as a stark reminder that safeguarding children in school settings requires constant vigilance and proactive policy enforcement. County officials have pledged to keep the public informed about the investigation’s progress, while advocacy groups continue to press for legislative reforms that would tighten oversight of youth sports. The outcome of Vassar’s trial could set a precedent for how similar allegations are addressed statewide, potentially reshaping the protocols that govern the relationship between educators, coaches, and the students they mentor.
